newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan blasts S.Africa for diplomatic breakup.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan blasts S.Africa for diplomatic breakup.

text.p: Taiwan's top envoy, having failed to rescue ties with South Africa, assailed Pretoria on Tuesday for betraying its democratic ideals and bowing to pressure to switch recognition to China.

Speaking after returning from his South Africa mission that included a secretive stopover in Belgium, Foreign Minister John Chang said he planned to visit Pretoria again in January but harboured no real hopes of salvaging formal relations.
"South Africa has abandoned its democratic principles in deciding to form ties with the autocratic government in mainland China," Chang told reporters.
"Our dignity was hurt and the mutual interests between our two countries were destroyed," Chang said.
South African President Nelson Mandela announced on November 27 that Pretoria, easily the biggest of Taiwan's diplomatic allies, would switch ties to Beijing in 1997.

The price of relations with Beijing is abandonment of ties with Taiwan, which China has regarded as a rebel province since a civil war split them in 1949. Beijing seeks to isolate Taiwan diplomatically in its quest for sovereignty over the island.
Chang left for Pretoria on December 2 hoping to reverse the decision but Mandela vowed to keep only close unofficial ties.
Mandela's refusal prompted Chang to announce angrily on Thursday that Taiwan would recall its ambassador and suspend all aid projects and treaties.

Seeking to put a positive spin to his diplomatic mission, Chang made a subsequent three-day transit stop in Belgium during which the minister said he "saw some friends" despite efforts by Chinese officials in Brussels to prevent all contacts.
"As soon as we got to our hotel in Brussels there already were officials from communist China checking on us," he said.
Chang declined to name the foreign officials he met in Brussels, which has formal ties with China, and admitted he "saw fewer friends than expected" because of China's pressure.
Chang said his South Africa trip in January would include damage-control visits to several African allies to ensure they do not follow Pretoria's lead and ditch Taipei for Beijing.
South Africa was likely lost for good, Chang said.

"We will not insist that South Africa change its mind because we know there is very little chance of that," Chang said. "But we hope to work out a formula for highest possible relations that would be acceptable to both sides."
He said Taipei would resume the suspended projects and treaties if the governments set a pact on bilateral relations.
He declined to say if Taipei would take the initiative to end formal ties if no agreements could be reached.
Taiwan's 30 allies are mostly underdeveloped states in the Pacific, Africa and central America that rely on it for aid.
Analysts warn that Pretoria's decision may encourage some friends to switch loyalty from Taipei to Beijing.
